claims.text: The quality and integrity of the native oxide film govern the corrosion behavior of Q235 steel in harsh environments.
Defects such as cracks or spalls in the oxide film permit aggressive attack and pitting in chloride-rich media.
Elevated temperature promotes corrosion through defects in the naturally formed oxide film.
Maintaining or modestly enhancing oxide-film integrity suppresses corrosion.
As-received commercial Q235 steel has a naturally developed native oxide layer.
Mechanical disruption of the oxide simulates a compromised protective film.
Mild anodic oxidation produces a thicker, more adherent passivating oxide film on Q235 steel.
Oxide-film continuity, thickness, composition, and microstructure are the structural mediators controlling corrosion behavior.
Chloride ions accelerate breakdown of a compromised oxide film through localized dissolution, cracking, and spallation.
Elevated thermal energy accelerates oxide-film breakdown.
Localized dissolution, cracking, and spallation lead to pitting and accelerated corrosion.
A robust, intact, or enhanced oxide film acts as a barrier that suppresses localized degradation.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, oxide-disrupted samples will have higher corrosion current density, lower impedance, more visible pitting, and greater weight loss.
The adverse effects of oxide disruption will be more pronounced at 60°C than at 25°C.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, samples with an enhanced oxide film will have lower corrosion current density, higher impedance, and fewer pitting sites.
Variation in native oxide composition and microstructural heterogeneity among commercial Q235 samples may affect absolute corrosion rates.
Electrochemical and morphological differences may be sensitive to small variations in processing and environmental conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as untreated Q235 tested at room temperature without aggressive chloride disruption, whereas the controlled comparisons and falsification study place the untreated reference in 3.5 wt% NaCl at both 25°C and 60°C. This leaves the operative reference condition ambiguous.
The material is described as being in a pre-exposure state, but the baseline calls it 'pre-exposed,' creating inconsistent exposure-state terminology.
